rows.title: Grant-funded streets and utilities for a Habitat neighborhood
rows.what_happened: Habitat for Humanity of Goldsboro-Wayne is building McNair Heights on 24.5 acres. Golden LEAF's grant served as the match for the City's CDBG infrastructure money, covering water, sewer, road, sidewalk and stormwater work. Phase 1 is 31 single-family homes: 25 Habitat homes and the rest sold on the open market.
rows.who_paid: Golden LEAF Foundation $500,000 (awarded 2025); City of Goldsboro CDBG and Habitat funds (amounts not stated). Infrastructure work is approximately $2.1 million; total project cost not stated.
rows.timeline: Golden LEAF award 2025; five houses under construction as of July 2026; built in phases
rows.lesson: Use a foundation grant as the local match for CDBG so a nonprofit builder does not have to carry the cost of streets and utilities.

rows.title: State disaster-recovery money pays for 40 apartments in a small town
rows.what_happened: The NC Office of Recovery and Resiliency awarded White Oak Landing Apartments, a 40-unit complex in Maysville, through the third round of its Affordable Housing Development Fund. The developer is Carolina Statewide Development, LLC. The money comes from federal CDBG-Disaster Recovery funds for Hurricanes Matthew and Florence.
rows.who_paid: NCORR Affordable Housing Development Fund (HUD CDBG-DR) $9,725,000. Total project cost not stated.
rows.timeline: awarded October 2023
rows.lesson: In a federally declared disaster area, even a town of under 1,000 people landed a 40-unit project once a developer applied for the recovery funds.
rows.source_name: NC Department of Public Safety / NCORR press release (Oct. 31, 2023)

rows.title: Teacher apartments paid for with a credit union loan and local shares
rows.what_happened: Bertie County's schools foundation built Dream Pointe Apartments, 24 two-bedroom units that can house up to 40 teachers. The project was first requested in 2017 and approved in 2019, then stalled during the pandemic before being revived. Rent is $800 a month, $104 below the $904 fair market rent.
rows.who_paid: SECU Foundation loan $3.1 million; Golden LEAF Foundation grant $527,000; Town of Windsor, Bertie County and the school district $160,000 each.
rows.timeline: requested 2017, approved 2019, opened July 2024
rows.lesson: Three modest equal shares, from the county, the town and the school district, closed the gap left after a zero-interest loan and a grant.

rows.title: County money plus a low-rate bank loan add 12 teacher units
rows.what_happened: Dare County commissioners approved just over $1 million for the Dare Education Foundation to add 12 teacher housing units on a 5.3-acre site in Kill Devil Hills. The foundation already runs 24 units in Kill Devil Hills (built 2008) and 12 in Buxton (built 2011) and has paid off those mortgages. Current units rent for $1,050 to $1,300 a month; the new ones are expected to rent for about $1,500.
rows.who_paid: Dare County just over $1 million; TowneBank $100,000 gift; TowneBank loan up to $3.5 million at 2.9%. Project capped at $4.65 million.
rows.timeline: approved July 2026; about 15 months of construction; move-in targeted fall 2027
rows.lesson: Once a nonprofit has paid off earlier units, a one-time county contribution can let it borrow for the next phase and repay from rents.

rows.title: City acts as bond conduit for a 144-unit complex
rows.what_happened: Morganton City Council voted to start the process of issuing up to $12 million in multifamily housing revenue bonds for Leonhardt Landing, 144 apartments on about 25 acres for households at 30% to 70% of area median income. The city is a conduit issuer: the developer, Sari and Co., repays the debt, not the city. The city collects a 1% fee of $120,000 and can withdraw if the project is not funded.
rows.who_paid: Up to $12 million in tax-exempt housing revenue bonds issued through the city and repaid by the developer; developer said as much as $15 million in federal Helene recovery funds may be available. Total cost not stated.
rows.timeline: site rezoned November 2025; construction expected second quarter 2027; substantial completion targeted December 2028
rows.lesson: A city can issue conduit housing bonds for a private developer without putting its own budget or credit at risk.

rows.title: Tribe combines three funding sources to build 30 homes for sale
rows.what_happened: The Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina received a state disaster-recovery award to build 30 single-family homes for ownership in its service area (Robeson, Scotland, Hoke and Cumberland counties). The homes target households at or below 80% of area median income, with some set aside for veterans and people with physical disabilities.
rows.who_paid: NCORR Affordable Housing Development Fund (CDBG-DR) $7,425,000 of an $11,016,500 total; the rest from Native American Housing Assistance and Self Determination Act funds and local HUD CDBG funds (amounts not stated).
rows.timeline: awarded October 2023
rows.lesson: Disaster-recovery housing funds can pay for homes for sale as well as rentals, when a local body brings its own federal housing dollars as match.
rows.source_name: NC Department of Public Safety / NCORR press release (Oct. 31, 2023)

rows.title: County government leads a 55-unit rental project
rows.what_happened: Scotland County, working with Southeastern Community Action Partnership, was awarded state disaster-recovery funds for the 55-unit I. Ellis Johnson multifamily rental project. The county itself is the lead applicant rather than a private developer.
rows.who_paid: NCORR Affordable Housing Development Fund (CDBG-DR) $9,656,244; also NC Housing Finance Agency Supportive Housing American Rescue Plan funds and bank loans (amounts not stated). Total cost not stated.
rows.timeline: awarded October 2023
rows.lesson: Where no developer is active, the county can be the applicant and partner with a community action agency to carry the project.
rows.source_name: NC Department of Public Safety / NCORR press release (Oct. 31, 2023)

rows.title: Recovery grant fills about half the cost of a tax-credit complex
rows.what_happened: Mills Property Development received a state disaster-recovery award for Pamlico Grove, a 56-unit apartment complex. The award funds 29 of the units; federal tax credits and bank loans cover the rest.
rows.who_paid: NCORR Affordable Housing Development Fund (CDBG-DR) $6,688,212 of a $13,575,566 total; federal tax credits and bank loans for the remainder.
rows.timeline: awarded October 2023
rows.lesson: In a small county, tax credits alone may not close the deal; expect a second public source of roughly half the cost.
rows.source_name: NC Department of Public Safety / NCORR press release (Oct. 31, 2023)

rows.title: County applies for water and sewer grant for a nonprofit's 33 homes
rows.what_happened: Jackson County Economic Development received a Golden LEAF grant for water and sewer infrastructure serving the Mountain Projects portion of Webster Village. Mountain Projects, a nonprofit that owns the land, plans 33 affordable single-family homes for local workers. The larger Webster Village plan also includes multifamily workforce and senior housing.
rows.who_paid: Golden LEAF Foundation $500,000 (Open Grants Program) for water and sewer. Total project cost and other funders not stated.
rows.timeline: grant awarded April 2026
rows.lesson: Jackson County's economic development office was the grant applicant for utilities serving a nonprofit's housing site.
rows.source_name: Golden LEAF Foundation grant listing: Webster Village

rows.title: Donated land and a community college build 44 small homes
rows.what_happened: The nonprofit Open Hearts Place broke ground on Hildebran Switch, 44 homes of 650 to 1,400 square feet on 6.2 acres donated by a local builder. Three homes are for the nonprofit's housing program and the rest will be sold at attainable prices to workers and seniors. Western Piedmont Community College construction classes are among the partners.
rows.who_paid: Land (6.2 acres) donated by Ken Orndorff of Piedmont Building Partners; nonprofit fundraising goal of $200,000 from donors, with grants pending. Total cost not stated.
rows.timeline: groundbreaking May 2025; up to four homes hoped for in the first year; two dozen homes in phase one
rows.lesson: With donated land and community college construction students, a small-home project started before major grants arrived.

rows.title: Regional loan fund backs 84 apartments in Haywood County
rows.what_happened: Mountain Housing Opportunities broke ground on Balsam Edge, 84 one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments on Howell Mill Road for households at 40% to 60% of area median income. It is among the first projects supported by the Western North Carolina Affordable Housing Loan Fund, launched in 2025 with an initial $40 million from Dogwood Health Trust through Self-Help.
rows.who_paid: Western North Carolina Affordable Housing Loan Fund (seeded with $40 million from Dogwood Health Trust via Self-Help Ventures Fund and Self-Help Credit Union); the loan amount for this project is not stated.
rows.timeline: groundbreaking March 2026; completion date not released
rows.lesson: A regional loan fund seeded by a health foundation can supply the gap financing that small mountain towns cannot raise alone.

rows.title: 42 income-limited rentals under construction in Brevard
rows.what_happened: Officials broke ground on Fairhaven Meadows, 42 rental units for households earning 40% to 70% of area median income. The project involves multiple partners.
rows.who_paid: Not stated in source.
rows.timeline: groundbreaking August 2025; move-in expected October 2026
rows.lesson: With partners lined up in advance, a project of about 40 units went from groundbreaking to move-in in a little over a year.

rows.title: Helene recovery funds for 55 apartments in Ashe County
rows.what_happened: Arendell Trace, a 55-unit rental development in West Jefferson, was one of 10 projects awarded through the state's Rental Production Program for Disaster Recovery. The program pairs CDBG-Disaster Recovery money with Low-Income Housing Tax Credits. Units must stay affordable for at least 30 years.
rows.who_paid: Rental Production Program for Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) $8,481,900, combined with NC Housing Finance Agency tax credits. Total cost not stated. Statewide round: more than $69 million for 828 units in 10 counties.
rows.timeline: awarded August 2026; awards must be committed by Oct. 30, 2030 and funds spent by Jan. 28, 2031
rows.lesson: Counties in the Helene disaster area should have a tax-credit project ready, because recovery dollars are awarded on top of tax credits.
rows.source_name: Office of the Governor press release (Aug. 25, 2026)

rows.title: Helene recovery funds for 93 apartments in Watauga County
rows.what_happened: Hemlock Ridge Trace, a 93-unit rental development in Boone, received one of the larger awards in the state's Rental Production Program for Disaster Recovery. The units must stay affordable for at least 30 years.
rows.who_paid: Rental Production Program for Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) $11,406,600, combined with NC Housing Finance Agency tax credits. Total cost not stated.
rows.timeline: awarded August 2026; funds must be spent by Jan. 28, 2031
rows.lesson: Disaster-recovery awards in this round ranged from under $2 million to over $13 million per project, so the ask should match the real gap.
rows.source_name: Office of the Governor press release (Aug. 25, 2026)

rows.title: Church uses a small grant to plan 12 units on its own land
rows.what_happened: Roanoke Island Presbyterian Church plans 12 workforce housing units for teachers, EMTs and other public service workers on its 2-acre property. It received the Outer Banks Community Foundation's first Focus Grant to pay for a feasibility study, initial architectural plans and site design. Fundraising for construction starts after that work is done.
rows.who_paid: Outer Banks Community Foundation Focus Grant of up to $50,000 for pre-development. Construction cost not stated.
rows.timeline: grant awarded 2025; no construction date set
rows.lesson: A small pre-development grant can turn land a church or civic group already owns into a buildable housing plan.

rows.title: City hires UNC's DFI to rank sites before seeking a developer
rows.what_happened: Hendersonville engaged UNC's Development Finance Initiative in 2024. DFI did a housing needs assessment, inventoried city-owned, county-owned and privately listed land, and modeled the cost to build and operate affordable housing on each site. The city's next steps are to prioritize sites, study one or more in depth and secure an experienced private partner.
rows.who_paid: Not stated in source.
rows.timeline: engaged 2024; site prioritization and developer search to follow
rows.lesson: Before asking for developer proposals, know which public sites pencil out and how much gap funding each would need.

rows.title: FEMA funds rebuilding of 50 flooded affordable homes
rows.what_happened: FEMA awarded funds to the Hendersonville Affordable Housing Corporation for Lincoln Circle and Robinson Terrace, where 50 homes were total losses in the Helene flooding of September 2024. The homes will be demolished and rebuilt.
rows.who_paid: FEMA: $16.8 million in federal funding expected to help rebuild the homes.
rows.timeline: FEMA announcement August 2026; new units expected in about two years
rows.lesson: Federal rebuilding money for damaged affordable housing arrived nearly two years after the storm, so plan interim housing for that long.

rows.title: Land trust builds 50 storm-resistant homes after Helene
rows.what_happened: Fuller Center Disaster ReBuilders and its Roots Community Land Trust broke ground on Heartwood Village, 50 permanently affordable homes on 10 acres for people displaced by Helene and essential workers. The land trust keeps the land; families buy the homes and resale terms keep them affordable for the next buyer. Homes are built to the FORTIFIED Gold standard.
rows.who_paid: Not stated in source.
rows.timeline: groundbreaking October 2026; first move-in expected summer 2027; all 50 homes occupied by 2029
rows.lesson: Putting rebuilt homes in a land trust keeps the public and donated money working for each later buyer.

rows.title: Residents and a local nonprofit buy mobile home parks as co-ops
rows.what_happened: In Emma, residents of a mobile home park bought it and turned it into a co-op about a decade ago. The nonprofit PODER Emma has since helped fund the purchase of five more parks that are now cooperatively owned, and has helped more than 45 mobile home owners with repairs. A newly bought parcel is planned as a new resident-owned park.
rows.who_paid: Invest Appalachia financed the latest land purchase with a bridge loan, a loan guarantee and a recoverable grant (amounts not stated); long-term refinancing sought from Seed Commons.
rows.timeline: first park bought about a decade ago; latest parcel bought in December before the July 2026 article
rows.lesson: Park purchases move on a seller's timeline, so line up a bridge lender before a park comes up for sale.

rows.title: County housing trust fund pays for repairs and small projects
rows.what_happened: Chatham County's Housing Trust Fund has provided over $2.6 million since 2018 for affordable housing preservation and development. Projects include converting the Siler Square School into housing, new apartments in Pittsboro and Siler City, supportive housing at the Farm at Penny Lane, and home repairs countywide. Nonprofits and developers apply each year.
rows.who_paid: Chatham County Housing Trust Fund: over $2.6 million since 2018 (per-project amounts not listed on the page).
rows.timeline: fund operating since 2018; annual application cycle
rows.lesson: A few hundred thousand county dollars a year is enough to serve as the local commitment that tax-credit and repair programs require.

rows.title: Nonprofit builds 26 mixed-income townhomes on a long-vacant lot
rows.what_happened: WeBuild Concord completed Lincoln Street Townhomes, 26 three-bedroom townhomes in Logan, the city's oldest and largest Black community, on a lot that sat vacant for 20 years. Nineteen homes are priced as affordable and five are market rate; some carry 99-year deed restrictions and some go into a community land trust.
rows.who_paid: About $6 million total, with part covered by American Rescue Plan dollars (amount not stated).
rows.timeline: groundbreaking 2022; completed January 2025
rows.lesson: Mixing market-rate and deed-restricted homes on one site lets a nonprofit build for-sale housing in a neighborhood under price pressure.

rows.title: Land trust homes sell for a fraction of the market median
rows.what_happened: Community Home Trust, a Chapel Hill nonprofit, owns the land under its homes and sells only the house; buyers agree to cap their resale price. Its director reports a median Community Home Trust home price of $130,000, against a private market median of $600,000 in Chapel Hill and Carrboro. The organization has operated for more than 30 years with municipal and county partners.
rows.who_paid: Not stated in source; works with the Town of Chapel Hill and other local governments.
rows.lesson: A land trust keeps each subsidized home affordable through every resale, so the public pays once.
rows.source_name: Chapelboro (Sept. 9, 2025; opinion piece by the organization's director)

rows.title: City puts $5 million into anti-displacement programs
rows.what_happened: Charlotte City Council approved $5 million to carry out six recommendations from its Neighborhood Equity and Stabilization (NEST) Commission. They include expanding acquisition-rehab-resale and House Charlotte Plus, an accessory dwelling unit program, repair help for small landlords in exchange for deed-restricted rents, and a shared ownership pilot.
rows.who_paid: City of Charlotte $5 million from the federal Coronavirus State and Local Fiscal Recovery Fund; must be spent by Dec. 31, 2026.
rows.timeline: approved November 2023; funds to be spent by end of 2026
rows.lesson: A resident commission turned one-time federal money into a short list of specific anti-displacement programs.

rows.title: Voter-approved bonds keep a housing trust fund going for 20 years
rows.what_happened: Charlotte created its Housing Trust Fund in 2001. Over two decades it has put more than $231 million toward creating and preserving more than 11,000 affordable units, mostly as gap financing for tax-credit rentals. Voters approved $50 million in housing bonds in 2020 and in 2022, then $100 million in 2024.
rows.who_paid: City of Charlotte housing bonds: $50 million (2020), $50 million (2022), $100 million (2024); more than $231 million invested through the fund overall.
rows.timeline: fund created 2001; latest bond approved November 2024
rows.lesson: Going back to voters on a regular schedule gives developers a gap-financing source they can plan around.

rows.title: City pays about $12,000 a unit to keep 292 apartments affordable
rows.what_happened: Raleigh approved $3.5 million to preserve five existing affordable rental developments: Avonlea (44 units), Jeffries Ridge (32), Madison Glen (120), Ripley Station (48) and Tryon Grove (48). Rents range from $735 to $1,355, and 62 of the units are supportive housing.
rows.who_paid: City of Raleigh $3,504,000 across five developments ($384,000 to $1,440,000 each).
rows.timeline: approved November 2023
rows.lesson: Keeping existing affordable apartments can cost far less per unit than building new ones.

rows.title: County loan attracts bank money for a $61.6 million preservation fund
rows.what_happened: Wake County put a $10.5 million loan into an Affordable Housing Preservation Fund run by Self-Help Ventures Fund, and Raleigh added $4 million. Commitments from Truist, First Horizon and Wells Fargo brought the total to $61.6 million. The fund makes short-term and permanent loans to buyers who keep existing apartments affordable, with a goal of 3,170 units over 15 years.
rows.who_paid: Wake County $10.5 million loan; City of Raleigh $4 million; Truist, First Horizon and Wells Fargo for the balance (individual amounts not stated). Total $61.6 million.
rows.timeline: announced October 2021; 15-year preservation goal
rows.lesson: Placed as a loan with a nonprofit lender, public money drew several times as much bank capital.

rows.title: Nonprofit renovates a 1965 complex to keep 50 low-rent units
rows.what_happened: Preservation of Affordable Housing, a nonprofit, closed financing and began a $4.7 million renovation of the 50-unit Biltmore Hills apartments in Southeast Raleigh. The city lists the project among four developments that closed financing in summer 2026.
rows.who_paid: $4.7 million renovation; individual funders and amounts not stated in the source.
rows.timeline: financing closed and work began July 2026
rows.lesson: To keep an older low-rent complex, help a nonprofit buyer close financing before the property sells to a market-rate owner.
rows.source_name: Preservation of Affordable Housing, summarizing News & Observer (July 20, 2026)

rows.title: Bond-backed rebuild of public housing reserves units for former residents
rows.what_happened: Durham opened The Vanguard, 72 mixed-income apartments, and broke ground on Dillard Street Apartments, 146 affordable and market-rate homes, as part of a four-phase redevelopment of 519 E. Main St. and Liberty Street Apartments. Twenty-one Vanguard units and 64 Dillard Street units are set aside for former residents.
rows.who_paid: Financed in part by Durham's voter-approved Forever Home bond initiative, with NC Housing Finance Agency, HUD Choice Neighborhoods and several banks (amounts not stated).
rows.timeline: Vanguard opened and Dillard Street broke ground September 2025; two more phases to come
rows.lesson: When redeveloping older subsidized housing, reserve units for the households who lived there and say how many up front.

rows.title: Land trust sells its first home at half of appraised value
rows.what_happened: The Asheville-Buncombe Community Land Trust sold its first home, a three-bedroom house in the Shiloh neighborhood, for $125,000 against a $250,000 appraisal. The trust keeps the land and sells the house to a buyer at or below 80% of area median income. The city dedicated $1 million from its 2016 housing bond to the trust in 2018, which paid for many of its property purchases.
rows.who_paid: City of Asheville: $1 million from the 2016 affordable housing bond, dedicated in 2018. Other sources not stated.
rows.timeline: city funding 2018; home acquired 2020; first sale July 2022
rows.lesson: A land trust needs seed money and years of lead time before its first sale, so fund it well ahead of need.
rows.source_name: Asheville Citizen Times via Yahoo News (Oct. 5, 2022)

rows.title: County lends $2 million to get 236 rent-restricted townhomes
rows.what_happened: New Hanover County approved a $2 million note at 5% interest to Cape Fear Development for Proximity Blue Clay, 236 townhomes for households at 60% to 90% of area median income. All units carry 10-year rent restrictions and the project uses no federal tax credits. Projected one-bedroom rent is about $1,311 against a market rent of $1,828.
rows.who_paid: New Hanover County $2 million loan at 5% annual interest, principal due after 10 years (about $1 million in interest to the county). Total project cost not stated.
rows.timeline: approved July 13, 2026; completion expected in about 18 months
rows.lesson: Lending rather than granting buys rent limits for middle-income workers, and the money comes back to the county.

meta.value: North Carolina housing projects and programs, 2021-2026, compiled for this dashboard. Every figure is from the linked source; blank means the source did not state it.
